subject: Accounting
title: Types of Financial Fraud
description: Learn Types of Financial Fraud in one minute.

hook.text: Fraud isn't just embezzlement. It includes fake invoices, inflated revenues, ghost employees, and more.

buildup.text: The three main categories are asset misappropriation, financial statement fraud, and corruption.

discovery.text: Asset theft is the most common but causes the smallest losses. Statement fraud is rarest but most costly.

twist.text: Corruption—kickbacks, bribery, conflicts of interest—sits in between and is hardest to detect.

climax.text: Understanding fraud types helps forensic accountants know exactly where to look for evidence.

punchline.text: Know the fraud types. That's where the trail begins.

quiz.question: Which type of fraud causes the largest financial losses?

details.summary: Financial fraud encompasses a wide range of schemes from simple embezzlement to complex financial statement manipulation. This topic categorizes the major fraud types, explains how each works, and identifies who typically commits each kind.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the landscape of fraud types helps organizations focus prevention efforts and helps forensic accountants recognize what they're looking for during investigations.
takeaways: The three main categories are asset misappropriation, financial statement fraud, and corruption
Asset misappropriation is the most common but least costly; financial statement fraud is rarest but most expensive
The median loss from financial statement fraud is over $500,000—ten times more than asset misappropriation

faq.question: What are the main types of financial fraud?
faq.answer: The ACFE classifies fraud into three categories: asset misappropriation (stealing company resources—most common at 86%), corruption (kickbacks, bribery, conflicts of interest—50%), and financial statement fraud (manipulating reported results—least common at 9% but most costly).

faq.question: Who typically commits each type of fraud?
faq.answer: Asset misappropriation is usually committed by lower-level employees skimming cash or submitting false expenses. Financial statement fraud is committed by senior management manipulating earnings. Corruption typically involves mid-to-upper management in purchasing or contracting roles.
